R1.e: Understand is a non-action verb, so we don't usually use it in the continuous form. Use the present simple: I don't understand.

R1.q: Sushi is made with fish that isn't cooked. The fish is ___.
R1.e: Raw food is not cooked at all. Roast, fried and baked food is cooked.

R1.q: A: This bag is really heavy. B: I ___ carry it for you.
R1.e: We use will ('ll) for offers and decisions we make at the moment of speaking.

R1.q: Giulia never gets angry when she has to wait. She's very ___.
R1.e: A patient person can wait calmly without getting angry.

R1.q: We ___ our old car last month.
R1.e: Last month is a finished time in the past, so we use the past simple, not the present perfect.

R1.q: The shop ___ me five euros for a plastic bag!
R1.e: The shop charges you money (asks you to pay). A thing costs money; a person pays or spends money.

R1.q: I ___ this phone for three years and it still works perfectly.
R1.e: Have (= possess) is a non-action verb, so we use the present perfect simple with for, not the continuous.

R1.q: The view from the top of the hill was absolutely ___.
R1.e: We use absolutely with strong adjectives like wonderful. With normal adjectives (good, nice) we use very.

R1.q: Which is ___ way to get to the airport: bus, train or taxi?
R1.e: We compare three things, so we need the superlative: the + adjective + -est.

R1.q: ___ life in a big city can be stressful.
R1.e: We don't use an article with uncountable nouns when we talk about things in general: Life is...

R1.q: Look! The chef ___ (make) pasta by hand.
R1.e: Look! shows the action is happening now, so we use the present continuous: is making.

R1.q: Your aunt's and uncle's children are your c___.
R1.e: The children of your aunt and uncle are your cousins.

R1.q: I ___ (never / win) any money in a competition.
R1.e: We use the present perfect with never to talk about experiences in our life: have never won.

R1.q: A train that travels under the ground in a city: the u___
R1.e: In London the underground train is also called the Tube.

R1.q: I'm very proud ___ my daughter. (Write the preposition.)
R1.e: We say proud of someone or something.

R2.q: In the UK, you ___ drive on the left.
R2.e: It's a rule, so it is necessary: have to. Mustn't and shouldn't mean the opposite.

R2.q: It's a secret. You ___ tell anyone!
R2.e: Mustn't means it is not allowed / don't do it. Don't have to means it isn't necessary.

R2.q: Nobody answered, so I left a ___.
R2.e: A voicemail is a spoken message you leave when someone doesn't answer the phone.

R2.q: I haven't ___ sleep well recently because of the heat.
R2.e: Can has no present perfect form, so we use have been able to.

R2.q: Luckily, the firefighters ___ rescue everyone from the building.
R2.e: For one successful action in the past we use was / were able to, not could.

R2.q: I'm very ___ in history, so I love visiting museums.
R2.e: -ed adjectives describe how a person feels: I'm interested. -ing adjectives describe the thing: history is interesting.

R2.q: While we ___ volleyball on the beach, it started to rain.
R2.e: We use the past continuous for a longer action in progress when another shorter action happened.

R2.q: By the time the referee blew the final whistle, half the fans ___ home.
R2.e: We use the past perfect for an action that happened before another past action: had left.

R2.q: The score was one-all at the end of the match. It was a ___.
R2.e: When both teams have the same score at the end, the match is a draw.

R2.q: When I was little, we ___ spend every summer at my grandparents' house by the sea.
R2.e: We can use would + verb for repeated actions in the past: we would spend...

R2.q: Students ___ (not have to) wear a uniform at our school.
R2.e: Don't have to means it isn't necessary, but you can if you want.

R2.q: The film had a really ___ (surprise) ending. Use -ed or -ing.
R2.e: The ending is the thing that surprises us, so we use the -ing adjective: surprising.

R2.q: The person who trains a sports team: a c___
R2.e: A coach trains the players and helps them improve.

R2.q: I ___ (usually / walk) to school, but today I'm taking the bus.
R2.e: We use the present simple + usually for present habits. Usually goes before the main verb.

R2.q: Laura and Davide were together for two years, but they broke ___ last month.
R2.e: Break up means to end a romantic relationship.

R3.q: The Leopard is a famous Sicilian novel. It ___ by Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa.
R3.e: The book didn't write itself, so we use the passive: was + past participle (written).

R3.q: A film that makes you laugh is a ___.
R3.e: A comedy is a funny film. Horror films and thrillers are scary or exciting.

R3.q: You've been working all day. You ___ be exhausted.
R3.e: We use must when we are almost sure something is true, because of the evidence.
We use our teeth to bite and chew food.

R3.q: I won't go out ___ I've finished my homework.
R3.e: Until means up to the time when. I'll stay in, and I'll go out only after I finish.

R3.q: Maths, history and English are school ___.
R3.e: The things you study at school, like maths or history, are subjects.

R3.q: If I ___ taller, I'd play basketball.
R3.e: In the second conditional we use the past simple after if. With be we often use were for all persons.

R3.q: A house joined to one other house on one side is a ___ house.
R3.e: Semi-detached = joined on one side. Detached = not joined. Terraced = in a row, joined on both sides.

R3.q: I'm thinking of ___ a new job.
R3.e: After a preposition (of) we use the -ing form (gerund).

R3.q: 'What time does the shop close?' She asked me what time ___.
R3.e: In reported questions we use normal word order (subject + verb), no do / did, and we move the tense back.

R3.q: The winners ___ (announce) tomorrow. Use will + passive.
R3.e: Future passive: will be + past participle.

R3.q: If you ___ (not hurry), you'll miss the bus.
R3.e: First conditional: if + present simple, will + verb.

R3.q: If I ___ (have) more free time, I would learn the guitar.
R3.e: Second conditional: if + past simple, would + verb. It's an imaginary situation.

R3.q: A person who works for a company: an e___
R3.e: An employee works for a company. The company or person who pays them is the employer.

R3.q: Make a noun from pay: p___
R3.e: We often add -ment to a verb to make a noun: pay → payment.

R4.q: If we ___ earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train.
R4.e: Third conditional: if + past perfect (had left), would have + past participle.

R4.q: If you had told me about the party, I ___.
R4.e: Third conditional (imaginary past): the result clause uses would have + past participle.
For adjectives ending in consonant + y, change y to i and add -ly: easy → easily.

R4.q: How ___ sugar do you take in your tea?
R4.e: Sugar is uncountable, so we use how much.

R4.q: Very ___ people came to the meeting, so it was cancelled.
R4.e: People is plural and countable, so we use few. Very few means not many.

R4.q: My laptop is really slow. Try turning it off and on again to ___ it.
R4.e: To restart a device means to switch it off and then on again.

R4.q: The woman ___ car was stolen called the police.
R4.e: Whose shows possession: the woman's car → the woman whose car.

o: My sister, that lives in Rome, is a teacher.
My sister, who lives in Rome, is a teacher.
My sister who she lives in Rome is a teacher.
R4.e: In non-defining clauses (with commas) we can't use that. Use who for people. Don't repeat the subject (she).

R4.q: A place where you catch a train: a railway ___
R4.e: Railway station is a compound noun: two nouns together that make one idea.
The sentence is negative (haven't), so the tag is positive with the same auxiliary: have you?

R4.q: I ___ (not / fall) if I had been more careful.
R4.e: Third conditional result: would not have + past participle (fallen).

R4.q: There aren't e___ chairs for everyone.
R4.e: Enough goes before a noun and means as many as we need.

R4.q: To put photos from your phone onto the internet: u___
R4.e: Upload = put files onto the internet. The opposite is download.

R4.q: The room where you have a bath or shower: b___
R4.e: Bathroom is a compound noun: bath + room.

R4.q: Someone who kills another person: a m___
R4.e: A murderer is a person who commits murder.

T1.q: Anna ___ in a restaurant in Palermo every weekend.
T1.e: Every weekend shows a habit or routine, so we use the present simple: works.

T1.q: This cake ___ too sweet. I can't eat it.
T1.e: Taste (= have a flavour) is a non-action verb, so we use the present simple.

T1.q: Oranges, lemons and grapes are all types of ___.
T1.e: Oranges, lemons and grapes are fruit.

T1.q: What ___ this evening? Have you got any plans?
T1.e: We use the present continuous for future plans and arrangements.

T1.q: I made my decision last year: I ___ study medicine at university.
T1.e: The decision was made before now (last year), so it's a plan: be going to. Will is for decisions made at the moment of speaking.

T1.q: My cousin always thinks he's better than everyone else. He's so ___.
T1.e: An arrogant person thinks they are better or more important than other people.

T1.q: Your wife's brother is your ___.
T1.e: The brother of your husband or wife is your brother-in-law.

T1.q: I ___ my keys last night, and I still haven't found them.
T1.e: Last night is a finished past time, so we use the past simple: lost.

T1.q: She ___ a lot of money since she started her new job.
T1.e: With since + a starting point we use the present perfect.

T1.q: I haven't got enough cash. Can I pay by ___?
T1.e: We say pay by card or pay in cash.

T1.q: How long ___ your best friend? Since primary school.
T1.e: Know is a non-action verb, so we use the present perfect simple (not continuous) with how long.

T1.q: You're all wet! What ___?
T1.e: We use the present perfect continuous for a recent activity that explains the present situation (you're wet).

T1.q: The film was absolutely ___. I laughed all the way through!
T1.e: Hilarious is a strong adjective (= very funny), so it can go with absolutely.

T1.q: I was absolutely ___ when I heard I'd won the prize. I couldn't believe it!
T1.e: Amazed is a strong adjective (= very surprised). We use absolutely with strong adjectives.

T1.q: I ___ (not / understand) what you mean.
T1.e: Understand is a non-action verb, so we use the present simple, not the continuous.

T1.q: Bread and cakes are cooked in the oven. They are b___.
T1.e: We bake bread and cakes in the oven.

T1.q: A: Oh no, I've forgotten my wallet! B: Don't worry. I ___ (lend) you some money.
T1.e: We use will for offers and quick decisions at the moment of speaking.

T1.q: To give money to someone that they will give back later: l___
T1.e: You lend money to someone. They borrow money from you.

T1.q: I've been learning English ___ six years.
T1.e: We use for with a period of time (six years) and since with a starting point (2020).

T1.q: She's tired because she ___ (run) for an hour. Use the present perfect continuous.
T1.e: Present perfect continuous: has / have + been + -ing.

T2.q: The train is ___ than the bus, but it's more expensive.
T2.e: Short adjectives add -er for comparatives: fast → faster than.

T2.q: This is ___ expensive car I've ever seen.
T2.e: Superlative of long adjectives: the most + adjective. We often use it with I've ever...

T2.q: My brother drives ___ carefully than me.
T2.e: Carefully is a long adverb, so the comparative is more carefully than.

T2.q: Cycling isn't as dangerous ___ people think.
T2.e: We use (not) as + adjective + as to compare.

T2.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: The flight was the more comfortable I've ever had.
The flight was most comfortable than the train.
The flight was the most comfortable I've ever had.
T2.e: With I've ever had we need the superlative: the most comfortable.

T2.q: On a plane you must fasten your seat ___.
T2.e: A seat belt keeps you safe in your seat in a car or plane.

T2.q: The roads are always busy at eight o'clock because it's ___ hour.
T2.e: Rush hour is the time when many people travel to and from work or school.

T2.q: The money you pay for a journey on a bus or train is the ___.
T2.e: A fare is the price of a journey. A fine is money you pay as a punishment.

T2.q: I'd like to be ___ doctor when I grow up.
T2.e: We use a / an with jobs. Doctor starts with a consonant sound, so a.

T2.q: My grandparents go to ___ church every Sunday.
T2.e: We don't use an article with church, school, hospital, etc. when we go there for its main purpose.

T2.q: I love ___ dogs, but I'm allergic to them.
T2.e: When we talk about things in general with plural nouns, we use no article.

T2.q: I'm not very keen ___ horror films.
T2.e: We say keen on something.

T2.q: My aunt is married ___ a man from Naples.
T2.e: We say married to someone.

T2.q: Don't be angry ___ me! It wasn't my fault.
T2.e: We say angry with a person and angry about a thing.

T2.q: Travelling by train is ___ (relaxing) than travelling by car.
T2.e: Relaxing is a long adjective, so the comparative is more relaxing.

T2.q: It was ___ (hot) day of the year.
T2.e: Superlative: the + adjective + -est. One vowel + one consonant: double it (hot → hottest).

T2.q: A person who travels to work or school every day: a c___
T2.e: A commuter travels a long way to work or school every day.

T2.q: She plays ___ piano very well. (Write the article.)
T2.e: We use the with musical instruments: play the piano, play the guitar.

T2.q: What do you usually spend your money ___? (Write the preposition.)
T2.e: We say spend money on something.

T2.q: A vehicle with two wheels and an engine: a m___
T2.e: A motorbike (or motorcycle) has two wheels and an engine. A bicycle has no engine.

T3.q: You ___ wear a seat belt in a car. It's the law.
T3.e: When something is a rule or law, it is necessary: have to.

T3.q: We ___ hurry. The film doesn't start for another hour.
T3.e: Don't have to = it isn't necessary. We have plenty of time.

T3.q: You ___ talk so loudly on the train. It's rude.
T3.e: We use shouldn't to give advice or say something is not a good idea.

T3.q: Which sentence is correct?
T3.e: Must doesn't change (no -s) and has no to after it. Have to changes: she has to.

T3.q: When I was at primary school, we ___ wear a uniform.
T3.e: Must has no past form. For obligation in the past we use had to.

T3.q: You need to ___ a number to make a phone call.
T3.e: To dial a number means to press the numbers to call someone.

T3.q: Please ___ your phone off during the exam.
T3.e: We say switch (or turn) your phone off / on.

T3.q: I ___ ride a bike when I was six.
T3.e: We use could for general ability in the past.

T3.q: I'd love to ___ play the piano.
T3.e: Can has no infinitive, so after would love to we use be able to.

T3.q: After three hours, we finally ___ find the hotel.
T3.e: For one specific success in the past we use was / were able to, not could.

T3.q: I've never ___ understand physics.
T3.e: Can has no present perfect, so we use have (never) been able to.

T3.q: I was so ___ that I fell asleep in front of the TV.
T3.e: -ed adjectives describe how a person feels: I was tired.

T3.q: The journey was really ___. We were in the car for nine hours!
T3.e: -ing adjectives describe the thing that causes the feeling: the journey was tiring.

T3.q: Are you ___ about the school trip?
T3.e: We use the -ed adjective for how a person feels: excited about something.

T3.q: You ___ (must / not) touch that. It's very hot!
T3.e: Mustn't = don't do it. It's dangerous or not allowed.

T3.q: Does your sister ___ (have to) wear a uniform at work?
T3.e: In questions with does, the verb stays in the base form: Does she have to...?

T3.q: The list of names and phone numbers in your phone: your c___
T3.e: Your contacts are the people and numbers saved in your phone.

T3.q: The signal was bad, and suddenly we got cut ___.
T3.e: If you get cut off, the phone call suddenly stops.

T3.q: I hope I ___ (be able to) come to your party next week. Use will.
T3.e: Can has no future form, so we use will be able to.

T3.q: That was the most ___ (bore) film I've ever seen!
T3.e: The film makes people feel bored, so we describe it with the -ing adjective: boring.

T4.q: I ___ my leg while I was skiing.
T4.e: We use the past simple for the short, finished action that happened during a longer one.

T4.q: She was nervous because she ___ in a big competition before.
T4.e: We use the past perfect for an experience before a moment in the past: had never played.

T4.q: At eight o'clock last night I ___ the match on TV, so I didn't hear the phone.
T4.e: We use the past continuous for an action in progress at a specific time in the past.

T4.q: The runners were tired because they ___ twenty kilometres.
T4.e: Past perfect: an action finished before another moment in the past (they were tired).

T4.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: He was scoring the goal while I bought a drink.
He scored the goal while I buy a drink.
He scored the goal while I was buying a drink.
T4.e: Use the past continuous for the longer background action (I was buying) and the past simple for the short action (scored).

T4.q: Our team ___ Palermo two-nil last Sunday.
T4.e: You beat a team or person. You win a match or competition.

T4.q: A tennis player hits the ball with a ___.
T4.e: Tennis players use a racket. In golf you use a club.

T4.q: Before a match, players ___ up by stretching and running slowly.
T4.e: Warm up means to prepare your body for sport with light exercise.

T4.q: I ___ like vegetables, but now I love them.
T4.e: Negative: didn't use to (no -d after didn't).

T4.q: My grandmother ___ tell us stories every night before bed.
T4.e: We can use would + verb for repeated actions in the past.

T4.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I would have a dog when I was a child.
I was used to have a dog.
I used to have a dog when I was a child.
T4.e: For past states (have, be, live) we use used to, not would.

T4.q: My brother ___ plays video games at the weekend.
T4.e: For present habits we use the present simple, often with usually.

T4.q: Chiara and Luca have been together for five years and now they're getting ___.
T4.e: Get married = become husband and wife.

T4.q: Sara and her best friend didn't talk for weeks after the argument, but now they've ___ up.
T4.e: Make up = become friends again after an argument.

T4.q: I ___ (not / see) the accident because I was looking at my phone.
T4.e: Past simple negative: didn't + base form.

T4.q: By the time we arrived, the game ___ (finish).
T4.e: The game finished before we arrived, so we use the past perfect: had + past participle.

T4.q: We ___ (use to / live) in a small flat in Palermo.
T4.e: Used to + verb for past states or habits that are not true now.

T4.q: Did you ___ (use to) go to the beach every summer?
T4.e: In questions with did, we write use to (no -d).

T4.q: To end a romantic relationship with someone: to b___ up with them
T4.e: Break up with someone = end a relationship.

T4.q: In basketball, you throw the ball into the b___.
T4.e: In basketball you score points by throwing the ball into the basket.

T5.q: Our house ___ at the moment, so we're staying with my aunt.
T5.e: Present continuous passive: is / are being + past participle, for something happening now.

T5.q: This bridge ___ in 1890.
T5.e: Past simple passive for a finished time in the past: was + past participle.

T5.q: A film full of fast cars, fights and explosions is an ___ film.
T5.e: An action film has lots of exciting scenes like fights and car chases.

T5.q: That ___ be Marco's car. He hasn't got a driving licence!
T5.e: We use can't when we are sure something is not true.

T5.q: Someone's at the door. It ___ be the postman, or maybe it's my brother.
T5.e: We use might when something is possible but we're not sure.

T5.q: You use your ___ to hold a pen.
T5.e: You hold a pen with your fingers.

T5.q: I'll text you as soon as the exam ___.
T5.e: After as soon as, when, until, etc. we use the present simple, even when we talk about the future.

T5.q: ___ you study, you won't pass.
T5.e: Unless means if... not: Unless you study = If you don't study.

T5.q: At the end of the school year, the teacher gives you a school ___.
T5.e: A school report shows your marks and progress (in Italian: la pagella).

T5.q: What would you do if you ___ the lottery?
T5.e: Second conditional: if + past simple, for imaginary situations.

T5.q: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ stay at home.
T5.e: This is a real possibility, so we use the first conditional: if + present, will + verb.

T5.q: We park the car in the ___ next to our house.
T5.e: A garage is a building where you keep your car.

T5.q: A house with only one floor is a ___.
T5.e: A bungalow is a house with only one floor (no stairs).

T5.q: If you want to become a doctor, you need to get a ___ in medicine.
T5.e: You get a degree when you finish a university course.

T5.q: English ___ (speak) all over the world. Use the present simple passive.
T5.e: Present simple passive: is / are + past participle.

T5.q: The person who writes the words that actors say in a film: a s___
T5.e: A scriptwriter (or screenwriter) writes the script of a film.

T5.q: He's got a big house and three cars. He ___ (must / be) rich.
T5.e: Must + base form when we are almost sure something is true.

T5.q: The part of your body between your head and your shoulders: n___
T5.e: Your neck connects your head to your shoulders.

T5.q: We won't start u___ everyone is here.
T5.e: Until means up to the time when. After until we use the present simple for the future.

T5.q: If I ___ (be) you, I'd apologise.
T5.e: Second conditional for advice: If I were you... (was is also possible in informal English).

T6.q: I've finished ___ my room.
T6.e: After finish we use the -ing form (gerund).

T6.q: My parents want me ___ a doctor.
T6.e: Want + person + to + verb: they want me to become.

T6.q: It's important ___ good communication skills.
T6.e: After It's + adjective we use to + infinitive.

T6.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I'm looking forward to meet you.
I'm looking forward to meeting you.
T6.e: In look forward to, to is a preposition, so it's followed by the -ing form.

T6.q: I promised ___ late again.
T6.e: Promise + to + verb. Negative: promise not to + verb.

T6.q: Before you get a job, the company may ask you to go for an ___.
T6.e: At a job interview the company asks you questions to decide if you are right for the job.

T6.q: She only works three mornings a week. She has a ___ job.
T6.e: A part-time job is only for some hours or days of the week.

T6.q: Last week Tom said, 'I'll help you tomorrow.' Tom said he ___ help me the next day.
T6.e: The promise was about a time that is now past, so will changes to would in reported speech.

T6.q: She asked me ___ I liked my new school.
T6.e: For reported yes / no questions we use if (or whether).

T6.q: He asked me where ___.
T6.e: In reported questions we use normal word order (subject + verb) and no did.

T6.q: 'I've lost my ticket.' She told me that she ___ her ticket.
T6.e: In reported speech the present perfect usually changes to the past perfect: had lost.

T6.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: He said me that he was busy.
He told that he was busy.
He told me that he was busy.
T6.e: Tell needs a person after it (told me). Say doesn't (he said that...).

T6.q: When a shop sells things at lower prices for a short time, there's a ___.
T6.e: A sale is a period when a shop sells things cheaper.

T6.q: The noun from decide is ___.
T6.e: Decide → decision. Many verbs ending in -de make nouns with -sion.

T6.q: I'm not very good at ___ (make) decisions.
T6.e: After a preposition (at) we use the -ing form.

T6.q: Can you help me ___ (carry) these boxes?
T6.e: After help we can use the base form or to + verb.

T6.q: To lose your job because you did something wrong: be f___
T6.e: If you are fired (or sacked), your boss makes you leave because of something you did.

T6.q: 'Are you tired?' Mum asked me after the long journey last night. She asked me if I ___ (be) tired.
T6.e: The question was about last night, so in the reported question the present (are) moves back to the past: was.

T6.q: Make a noun from explain: e___
T6.e: Explain → explanation. Note the spelling change: no i after the a.

T6.q: Something you buy for much less than its usual price is a b___.
T6.e: A bargain is something you buy cheaply, for less than it's worth.

T7.q: If I'd known you were ill, I ___ you some soup.
T7.e: Third conditional: if + past perfect (I'd known), would have + past participle.

T7.q: If she ___ her umbrella, she wouldn't have got wet.
T7.e: In the if clause of the third conditional we use the past perfect: had taken.

T7.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: If I would have seen you, I had said hello.
If I saw you, I would have said hello.
If I had seen you, I would have said hello.
T7.e: Third conditional: if + had + past participle, would have + past participle.

T7.q: We ___ the last bus if we had run faster.
T7.e: In the third conditional we can use could have instead of would have for possibility.

T7.q: The opposite of fortunately is ___.
T7.e: We add the prefix un- to make the opposite: unfortunately.

T7.q: The adverb from happy is ___.
T7.e: For adjectives ending in consonant + y, change y to i and add -ly: happily.

T7.q: The opposite of possible is ___.
T7.e: Many adjectives starting with p use the prefix im-: impossible, impatient, impolite.

T7.q: Make an adjective from danger: ___
T7.e: We add -ous to some nouns to make adjectives: danger → dangerous.

T7.q: I've got ___ money left, just enough for an ice cream.
T7.e: Money is uncountable, so we use a little (= some, but not much).

T7.q: There are ___ people on the beach today. There's no space to put my towel!
T7.e: People is plural and countable, so we use too many (= more than we want).

T7.q: I don't eat ___ fruit. I should eat more.
T7.e: Not enough = less than we need. Enough goes before the noun.

T7.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I haven't got no free time.
I have got any free time.
I haven't got any free time.
T7.e: In negative sentences we use any. We don't use two negatives (haven't + no) in English.

T7.q: Press this ___ to switch on the TV.
T7.e: You press a button to switch a device on or off.

T7.q: You look at the ___ of your phone to read messages.
T7.e: The screen is the part of the phone where you see pictures and text.

T7.q: If we ___ (not / get) lost, we would have arrived on time.
T7.e: Third conditional: if + past perfect. Negative: hadn't + past participle.

T7.q: She ___ (not / meet) her husband if she hadn't gone to that party.
T7.e: Third conditional result: would not have + past participle.

T7.q: Make an adverb from quick: q___
T7.e: Most adverbs of manner are adjective + -ly: quick → quickly.

T7.q: How ___ hours a day do you spend online?
T7.e: Hours is plural and countable, so we use how many.

T7.q: There were very f___ students in class today because of the flu.
T7.e: Very few = not many. We use few with plural countable nouns.

T7.q: A small, flat computer that you use by touching the screen: a t___
T7.e: A tablet is a small computer with a touch screen.

T8.q: That's the man ___ I saw at the station.
T8.e: We use who (or that) for people in relative clauses.

T8.q: The phone ___ I bought last week has stopped working.
T8.e: We use that or which for things. We can't use what as a relative pronoun.

T8.q: Is this the restaurant ___ you had your birthday party?
T8.e: We use where for places: the restaurant where...

T8.q: My best friend, ___ mother is a teacher, helps me with my homework.
T8.e: Whose shows possession: my friend's mother → my friend, whose mother...

T8.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: Bagheria, that is near Palermo, has beautiful villas.
Bagheria, which is near Palermo, has beautiful villas.
Bagheria, where is near Palermo, has beautiful villas.
T8.e: In a non-defining clause (with commas) we can't use that. Use which for things and places as subject.

T8.q: A place where you can leave your car: a car ___
T8.e: Car park is a compound noun: two nouns that make one idea (a place to park cars).

T8.q: The room where you sleep is the ___room.
T8.e: Bedroom is a compound noun: bed + room.

T8.q: You can swim, ___?
T8.e: Positive sentence → negative tag with the same auxiliary: can't you?

T8.q: He's never been to London, ___?
T8.e: Never makes the sentence negative, so the tag is positive: has he? ('s = has here).

T8.q: They were at home last night, ___?
T8.e: Positive past sentence with were → negative tag: weren't they?

T8.q: You don't like horror films, ___?
T8.e: Negative sentence with don't → positive tag: do you?

T8.q: The police are trying to find out who stole the painting. They are ___ the crime.
T8.e: To investigate a crime means to try to find out what happened and who did it.

T8.q: A person who robs banks is a ___.
T8.e: A robber steals from banks or people, often using violence. A burglar breaks into houses.

T8.q: If you are found guilty, the judge will give you a ___.
T8.e: A sentence is the punishment the judge gives, for example two years in prison.

T8.q: The girl ___ sits next to me is from Palermo. (Write one relative pronoun.)
T8.e: We use who or that for people in defining relative clauses.

T8.q: That's the shop ___ I bought my trainers. (Write one word.)
T8.e: We use where for places.

T8.q: It's a lovely day, ___? Write the question tag.
T8.e: Positive sentence with is → negative tag: isn't it?

T8.q: She'll come to the party, ___? Write the question tag.
T8.e: Positive sentence with will ('ll) → negative tag: won't she?

T8.q: The small book you show at the airport when you travel abroad: p___
T8.e: Passport is a compound noun: pass + port.

T8.q: When the police take someone to the police station because of a crime, they a___ them.
T8.e: To arrest someone means the police take them because they think they committed a crime.
